sessions.lastUserText: Yeah, we need to have, can we specify better to say that the hands are touching, and the right arm is crossed?

last.text:
**You were right, and I was wrong to call it not generable.**

Two complete cycles: closed and elbows-forward at 0s, 5s and 9s → up and back with the chest wide open at 2–3s and again at 7s → down and forward again. Forward, up, back, down. That's a backward shoulder roll.

And the thing that was missing in every previous attempt is there: **the chest visibly opens and closes.** At 2–3s her shoulder blades draw together and the chest is wide; at 0s and 5s the shoulders are rolled forward and closed. That's protraction and retraction of the girdle — the actual scapular movement, not an arm swing around a static shoulder.

**Your diagnosis was the right one.** Every start frame before this was a *neutral mid-position* — arms out to the sides, or hanging — which gives the model no information about where in the cycle it is or which way to go. The closed, elbows-forward pose puts her at the beginning of the circle, where "roll backwards" has only one possible continuation. The model didn't need a better description; it needed to be told where the movement starts.

Which means my conclusion two messages ago was drawn too early. I tested four models across two poses and concluded the capability was absent — but **both poses were mid-position poses**. I varied the models and the words and never varied the thing that mattered.

Two practical notes:

**720p cost ~110 cr against ~30 at 480p** — about 3.7×, a steeper jump than I'd assumed. Worth proving movements at 480p and only re-rendering keepers at 720p.

**And I'd still watch it before trusting it.** I'm reading 1fps stills; her head dips slightly at 3s and 7s, and there's some camera drift. Whether those matter needs your eyes.

If it holds up, the principle generalises to the whole library: **start every clip at the beginning of the movement, not in the middle of it.** That's a rule about how to generate all 88, and it's worth more than this one clip.

Balance 2,033.

last.text:
Ten movements, in order:

**On all fours (six of them)**

1. **Cat–cow** *(1:17)* — arching and rounding the spine, head dropping and lifting. Loosens the lower back.
2. **Side-body reach** *(1:53)* — one hand crossed in front of the other, hips pushed out to the opposite side into a banana shape, then moving the hips around to find the stretch down the side. Both sides.
3. **Thoracic rotation** *(2:31)* — one hand (or elbow, if the shoulder is stiff) reaches up to the ceiling, then threads back through under the body. Hips deliberately stay still so the movement comes from the mid-back. Both sides.
4. **Shoulder circles** *(3:46)* — one arm circling all the way round, or just the elbow if the full range is uncomfortable. Both sides.
5. **Hip circles, forward** *(5:33)* — knee lifts toward the tummy, circles out to the side and back down. Both sides.
6. **Hip circles, reverse** *(6:11)* — the same circle the other way, pushing the foot up toward the sky first, then round from back to front. Pelvis stays neutral, core engaged.

**Seated on the floor**

7. **Knee drops** *(4:22)* — sitting with feet on the floor wider than hip width, hands behind for support, dropping both knees toward the floor and back. Leaning further back makes it easier.

**Seated cross-legged**

8. **Neck — look down and across** *(7:24)* — sitting tall, looking down toward the opposite knee. Both sides.
9. **Neck — ear to shoulder** *(8:09)* — taking one ear toward the same shoulder while keeping the opposite shoulder down. Both sides.
10. **Seated side reach** *(8:43)* — one hand planted on the floor, the other arm reaching up and over into a side bend. Both sides.

Roughly eight minutes of actual movement, with the first minute and the last thirty seconds being talk. Every movement is bilateral except cat–cow and the knee drops.

The pattern worth noting: she works **spine → side body → mid-back → shoulders → hips → neck**, ending on the neck once everything else has moved.

**She's Dr. Stacy Sims** — exercise physiologist, author of *ROAR*/*Next Level*, the "women are not small men" person. All three clips had real captions, so no paid transcription was needed.

**Artifact:** https://claude.ai/code/artifact/09f8afce-857f-4774-a6d1-a14be3683f1e
**Hosted:** https://eugenechantk.me/pages/what-dr-stacy-sims-says-and-what-4c1f9e2a/

I read her against our actual twelve-week plan rather than just listing what she said. Headline findings:

**Most of what she preaches, we already do.** Mobility-first on-ramp, months-not-weeks before load, real objects over machines, compound functional patterns, consistency before content, convert-the-walk-you-already-take. Her *on-ramp* advice is essentially a description of our user — which is useful ammunition if the trainer pushes back on our conservatism.

**Our biggest gap is intensity, not rep ranges.** Her actual mechanism is reps-in-reserve: target ~6 reps with 2 left, and the default error is going too light. Our programme prescribes reps everywhere and intensity *nowhere* — one cue, in strength week 2, and it's a soft one. So we ramp volume (3×6→3×8→3×10) on a bag she picked once in week 5 and never revisits. That's a volume ramp on a static load, and nothing in the system notices. One question after a loaded set — *could you have done three more?* — fixes it with no new footage.

**We have the eccentric half and not the concentric half.** Our 4-second descents are good and she doesn't even mention them. But nothing anywhere says *move fast on the way up*. Power declines faster than strength with age and catching a stumble is a rate-of-force problem — arguably higher value for a 60-year-old than a heavier bag.

**One deliberate divergence worth knowing about:** her conditioning is 30s maximal + 2–3 min full recovery. Our energy block does the exact opposite — continuous circuits with *shrinking* rest. Ours is right for our user; I'd just rather we know we diverged than find out in trainer review.

Two cautions I put in the doc: her audience is 42 and has gym access, not 60 and deconditioned — take her principles, not her prescriptions. And her signature "10–12 reps stops working after 35" line is delivered with more certainty than the literature carries. Adopt the feedback mechanism, not the specific number.

Also pulled a section of copy angles — "you're the first generation of women to strength train" and "a wellness meeting with yourself, and we don't break meetings" are both unusually good for this audience.

Nothing in the programme was changed.

last.text:
Written up as `workout-videos/01-rock-your-hips/MOVEMENT.md`, alongside a rewritten motion script. Here's the substance.

## The joint action, in one sentence

The pelvis rotates as a **single rigid block** around a horizontal axis running side-to-side through both hip joints, while the femurs, ribcage and head stay put. The lumbar spine isn't driving — it's being *shaped* by the pelvis moving underneath it.

**Rolling back (the tuck):** the top of the pelvis tips backwards away from the thighs; the pubic bone rises toward the navel; the tailbone tucks down and forward underneath her; she rolls onto the rear edge of the sit bones and the contact point on the bed travels back 2–3 cm. The low back's inward hollow flattens, then goes gently convex. Front of the waist shortens.

**Rolling forward (the arch):** exact mirror. Tailbone lifts back and up behind her, pubic bone points at the floor, she rolls onto the front edge of the sit bones, and the hollow above the waistband deepens.

## What the camera actually sees change

This is the part that matters for prompting, because it's the part a model can render. Only one region of the silhouette changes shape — ribs to thighs — and it reads as three lines:

1. **The lower-back line** — hollow → flat → convex, and back. Primary tell, and the whole reason the shot is side-on.
2. **The waistband angle** — a straight line across the body tipping like a see-saw. On fitted sage loungewear this is the single most legible element in frame.
3. **The hands** — they sit on the moving bone, so they're a pointer: two clearly visible objects rotating through the same arc as a body part that's hard to see on its own.

Everything above the ribs and below the knees is a **static reference** the three read against. If the head or shoulders also travel, the eye loses the baseline and the movement becomes unreadable even when it's technically there.

## The one gate worth stating

The failure to prevent is a **hip hinge** — whole torso pivoting forward, head dropping, shoulders swinging. That's a seated forward fold, and it's exactly what Kling produced. The discriminator is blunt:

> In a correct pelvic tilt, **the head does not change position.** If the head moves through an arc, it's the wrong movement, however good it looks.

## Two things this makes me think are the actual blocker

Writing the spec out surfaced something your `RESULTS.md` flags as untested:

**True range is 10–15° each way — the top of the pelvis travels 2–4 cm.** In a full-body 3:4 frame at 480p that's roughly 15–25 px over four seconds. So the caveat in RESULTS is probably right, and there are two compounding levers, not one:

- **Exaggerate to 25–30°.** Demo footage exaggerates as a convention. "Smaller than you think" is a voiceover line, not a thing the demonstrator performs.
- **Crop tighter — mid-thigh to shoulders.** Your own house rule says *frame for the axis being demonstrated*. The full-body frame exists to satisfy the feet-flat cue, and that cue is currently costing you the entire movement. Feet-flat can live in the start frame or a 2-second wide establishing beat.

Also worth naming: the morning-three variant is explicitly *half* the session range, which makes **the pilot clip the smallest-amplitude version of the smallest-amplitude movement on the list.** The four failures are weaker evidence against AI generation than they look.

I've written `prompt-motion-v2-exaggerated.txt` — rewritten around described end-poses rather than instructions, negations converted to positive anchors ("as if there were a low shelf just above her head"), and the waistband and hands promoted to the explicit visual tell. It's ready for the Kling test that RESULTS lists as next, **~30 cr, ~14 min — say the word and I'll run it.** Nothing generated.

Want me to give the other 14 movements the same treatment? The three-lines-of-silhouette framing should transfer, but each one has a different discriminating failure.

---

last.text:
You're right, and the comparison makes it precise. Only about half actually match.

| Panel | Source | Generated | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | mid-sweep, one arm out, one trailing back | symmetric wide T | ✗ |
| 2 | hands together in front of chest | hands together at chest, prayer-ish | ~ |
| 3–5 | arms reaching forward, hands together | arms reaching forward | ✓ |
| 6 | mid-sweep, arms opening asymmetrically | symmetric wide T | ~ |
| 7 | standing, arms lowering | standing, arms at sides | ✓ |
| 8–11 | arms angling back behind the hips | arms hanging at sides, no travel | ✗ |
| 12 | near arm sweeping forward, far arm trailing | arms reaching forward | ~ |

**Two distinct causes**, and they need different fixes.

**Panels 8–11 — the known wall.** Arms-behind still doesn't render. Four routes have now failed on it and one has succeeded, so this isn't news, just confirmation.

**Panels 1, 6, 12 — a new problem I should have anticipated.** Those source frames are *mid-swing*: asymmetric, one arm leading and one trailing, motion blur on the hands. The model resolved every one of them into a tidy symmetric pose. It renders *positions*, not *moments in transit* — and three of your twelve frames are transit, not position.

That second one matters more than it looks. It means a 12-frame board sampled uniformly in time can't be reproduced frame-for-frame by an image model, because a third of those samples aren't poses at all — they're blurs between poses. The catalogue sampled every 0.75s precisely to show motion; that's what makes those frames unreproducible.

**What I think this tells us.** The 12-frame board was the wrong target. What the video model actually needs is the *phase boundaries* — the three or four positions the movement passes through — pinned exactly, with the transits left for it to interpolate. That's the segment plan, and this exercise is fairly strong evidence for it: the frames that reproduced cleanly are exactly the held positions, and the ones that failed are exactly the moments where the body is between positions.

So the honest read: this board is a good *reference document* for panels 3–5 and 7, and it demonstrates the character and set hold up across twelve panels. It is not a frame-accurate replica of the source rep, and I don't think any image model will produce one.

Two ways forward:

- **Build the board from the four real positions** (arms-forward, wide T, hands-behind, neutral), each generated as an edit from the master where we know it works, and treat those as the storyboard. Accurate, cheap, and directly usable as video endpoints.
- **Keep chasing all twelve** — but I'd want to say plainly I don't think panels 1, 6 and 12 are achievable, because they're pictures of movement rather than pictures of a pose.

Which do you want?

Albo is probably making around **$35K/month**, but this is estimated—not disclosed.

A defensible range is **$15K–$35K/month in App Store revenue**, or roughly **$180K–$420K annualized**:

- ScreensDesign currently shows **$35K/month and 65K monthly downloads**; an older snapshot on the same page shows $15K and 30K downloads. [ScreensDesign](https://screensdesign.com/showcase/albo-save-organise)
- Albo claims **250K+ users**. [Albo affiliate page](https://albo.inc/affiliate-program)
- Its main annual subscription is **$29.99**. [App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/albo-save-organize/id6578421992)
- At $35K revenue and 65K downloads, the implied purchase rate is approximately **1.8%**, consistent with the older snapshot’s ratio.
- The company was only incorporated in February 2025, and its first accounts are not due until November 2026, so there are no public financials yet. [Companies House](https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/company/16271351)

That is revenue, not profit. Payroll, AI extraction, infrastructure, App Store fees, and Albo’s 30% affiliate commission could consume much of it.

## Is link saving a good space?

**As a standalone category: mediocre. As an entry point into something more valuable: good.**

The core problem is genuine and widespread, but generic link storage has structural weaknesses:

- Browser bookmarks, Instagram/TikTok saves, Notion, and Apple Notes are free substitutes.
- People enjoy saving far more than revisiting, creating poor retention.
- Willingness to pay for “better storage” is limited.
- Social-content extraction is brittle when platforms change.
- AI processing creates variable costs.

The market can support strong indie businesses: mymind is estimated around **$880K ARR**, while Albo may be approaching a $400K annual revenue run rate. But Pocket shutting down despite having millions of users is an important warning: massive usage does not automatically create a sustainable business. [Mozilla’s Pocket announcement](https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/future-of-pocket)

My recommendation: **don’t build “another bookmark manager.”** Use saving as the capture mechanism, then monetize an outcome:

- Social recipes → meal planning and groceries
- Saved places → maps, itineraries and bookings
- Saved products → price tracking and affiliate commerce
- Saved knowledge → synthesis, creation and decision support

Albo itself appears to understand this: recent releases emphasize cook mode, grocery lists, maps, events, reviews, and social planning—not merely link storage.

**Verdict:** good space for a focused, profitable consumer app; questionable as a venture-scale category unless the saved-content graph becomes a transaction, creation, or social-discovery platform.
